idiom_name: package-private struct with unexported fields + NewOrder constructor
implementation_notes: Go's encapsulation is package-scoped: unexported struct fields are unreachable from other packages, so the root is a struct whose fields are lowercase and whose only mutation paths are exported methods - the constructor idiom (`NewOrder`, no Get prefix on getters) is what replaces a class initializer (Effective Go: constructors and composite literals). Parts are values owned by the root and copied in on the way in so the caller cannot retain a mutation handle, other aggregates are held by id, and persistence is explicit `database/sql` code inside one transaction, since the standard library has no ORM or unit of work. Because any field that is exported (or any composite literal inside the package) can bypass the root, the aggregate model belongs in its own package.
pitfalls: Privacy stops at the package boundary: any file in the same package can assign o.total directly, so keep exactly one aggregate per package (or treat exported fields inside the model package as a review red flag).

append and slicing share the backing array: storing a caller's slice without copying, or returning o.lines directly, lets outside code mutate the aggregate - copy on entry and on the way out (slices.Clone, Go 1.21+).
A struct value is copied on assignment; copying an aggregate that owns a mutex or an incrementally maintained total lets the copies diverge, so pass *Order and keep a single owner.

There is no unit of work in the standard library: the repository must load all parts and write root plus lines inside one `*sql.Tx`, and forget to delete removed children leaves rows the invariant will trip over on the next load.
